name: Ledgerline — the billable-work evidence trail for small professional-service firms
one_liner: For 3-30 person agencies and consultancies billing on retainers and SOWs, Ledgerline reads the client-facing email, calendar and ticket trail and produces a dated, source-linked record of what was requested, who requested it, what work followed and what fell outside scope — ready to attach to an invoice or a disputed-hours reply.
problem: Small agencies and consultancies bill monthly retainers or fixed SOWs, and the month's actual work lives scattered across Gmail threads, calendar invites, Slack DMs and a Jira/Asana board. When the client says "we never approved that" or "why is this invoice $9k", the account lead spends 2-6 hours digging through threads to rebuild what happened, and often just writes the hours off rather than fight. Today's workarounds are (a) manual time entry, which is retroactive and thin, (b) PSA tools like Teamwork, Harvest, Productive and Accelo, which are excellent once hours and change requests are logged in the product but useless for work that was agreed in an email at 7pm, and (c) passive timekeepers like Laurel and Smokeball AutoTime, which are enterprise/legal-priced, Windows-centric or quote-only. None of them answer the specific question a disputed invoice asks: show me, with links, the request, the approval and the work. Agent tooling finally makes this reconstructable: an agent can read a month of threads, cluster them into requests, and cite the exact message for each claim.
target_customer: Owner/principal or head of delivery at a 3-30 person digital, design, marketing or data-consulting firm billing $15k-$150k/month on retainers; they already pay $10-25/user/month for Harvest, Teamwork or Productive and own the invoicing decision personally. Secondary: boutique accounting and IT-MSP practices with the same retainer/scope pattern.
why_now: Two things changed in the last year. First, long-context models plus cheap Gmail/Calendar/Slack read-only connectors make reconstructing a month of client correspondence into a cited chronology a routine, under-a-dollar job rather than a research project — the Cursor Agent SDK launch (Oct 2026) and the proliferation of hosted agent frameworks mean the orchestration and eval tooling is off-the-shelf. Second, the "who did what on shared data" problem is now openly discussed by practitioners (sriramk's bookmark), and agents themselves are starting to act in clients' inboxes and calendars, so the provenance question is getting worse, not better. Incumbent passive-timekeeping leaders (Laurel, Smokeball AutoTime) remain quote-only and vertical-locked, leaving the sub-30-person non-legal market unserved.
comparables: Laurel (laurel.ai) — passive cross-app capture of email, docs, meetings; drafts narratives and assigns to matters/projects; serves legal, accounting and consulting; quote-only with no self-serve tier and reported implementation complexity and desktop-monitoring privacy concerns. Gap: no self-serve product for a 6-person agency, and it is built around timesheets, not scope evidence. Smokeball AutoTime (smokeball.com/features/do/autotime) — background activity tracking that drafts legal time entries; Windows-focused, no Google Workspace support, tier/add-on pricing opaque. Gap: legal-only, PC-only. Clio Duo (from ~$89/user/mo tiers) — AI assistance with time entries inside Clio; assistance, not reconstruction, and legal-only. Teamwork, Harvest, Productive, Accelo, Scoro — agency PSA and time tracking at $10-25/user/mo; strong when the team logs hours and change requests as work happens, with no capability to reconstruct a dispute from scattered email and chat. ActiveProspect TrustedForm ($0.15/certificate, $10/mo minimum) — the closest analogue in a different market: it proves consent with a stored, replayable record, which is the same "evidence artifact" business model Ledgerline would run for billable work. Gap left open across all of them: nobody sells a cheap, self-serve, read-only artifact that answers "prove this request was made and approved" for a small non-legal firm.
risks: 1) Access risk: client correspondence is the most sensitive mailbox a firm has, and a security review by a 6-person agency's biggest client can kill the deal; the forward/upload fallback is a partial answer but reduces coverage. 2) Accuracy risk in an adversarial setting: this output goes to a paying client, so one hallucinated "approval" destroys trust permanently — mandatory human review and quote-only claims make the product slower and less magical. 3) Incumbent absorption: Productive, Teamwork or Laurel can add "reconstruct from email" as a feature to a customer base already paying them, and the data access is a smaller ask for an incumbent that is already in the workflow.
riskiest_assumptions: 1) Firms will grant read access to the client-facing mailbox and calendar of 2-3 account leads. This is the hardest gate: it is client correspondence, sometimes under NDA. If they will not, the product dies; mitigation is a forward-only mode where they BCC/forward a label to Ledgerline, or a desktop-local first version. 2) The reconstruction is accurate enough to put in front of a client. A chronology that invents an approval is worse than no product, so every line must be a quote with a link and "no evidence found" must be a first-class output. 3) The pain is actually paid for, not absorbed. Agencies may simply write off disputed hours rather than buy a tool; I did not find direct evidence of budget for this exact job, only for adjacent PSA/time software.
first_customers: Ten owner-operated agencies the builder can reach directly: 4-5 from agency-owner communities that discuss scope creep openly (r/web_design, r/agency, the Parakeeto agency-profitability audience, Teamwork/Productive user groups on LinkedIn); 3 UiPath/automation partner shops in the builder's own network, who bill on SOWs and understand read-only connectors; 2 boutique design studios with 5-20 staff found via Clutch or Dribbble. Opening line: "send me one disputed invoice and the thread behind it, I'll send back the evidence pack free."
validation_test: This week: offer 10 agency owners a free "invoice defence pack". They forward one real client thread (an .mbox export or a forwarded thread chain) plus the SOW PDF; within 24 hours they get back a one-page dated chronology with each request, the requester, the approval quote, the work that followed, and an out-of-scope list with links. Pass = 6 of 10 send real material, and 3 of those say they would send the pack to the client or ask what it costs monthly. Fail = fewer than 3 send anything, or recipients say the chronology tells them nothing they did not already know. Run it by hand with a long-context model; no product required.
build_plan: Narrowest first version — "one month, one client, one PDF", no autonomous agent, no writes anywhere. (1) Read-only Google OAuth for Gmail + Calendar scoped to one label/one client domain, plus a drag-and-drop .eml/.mbox fallback so the first customers need no IT approval. (2) Upload the SOW or retainer scope as PDF; extract the in-scope deliverable list into a checklist. (3) Pipeline: thread → request-cluster → classify each cluster as request / approval / delivery / out-of-scope, each with a verbatim quote, timestamp, sender and permalink; anything unsupported is explicitly rendered as "no evidence found". (4) Human review screen: the account lead accepts, edits or deletes each line before anything is exported. (5) Export a client-ready PDF evidence pack plus a copyable invoice narrative. Cut for v1: Slack and Jira ingestion, time estimates and dollar amounts, multi-user seats, any write-back to a PSA, automatic monthly runs, anything that resembles employee activity monitoring.
reasoning:
Ledgerline wins the venture track because it is the only candidate where I found a named buyer who already spends money adjacent to the problem (agency PSA and time tracking at $10-25/user/month) and a gap that my research actually confirmed rather than assumed: the passive-capture leaders, Laurel and Smokeball AutoTime, are quote-only, enterprise-paced and legal/accounting-locked, while the agency PSA tools only work when hours and change requests were logged as the work happened — which is exactly what does not happen in a 6-person shop. The wedge is narrow and shippable: one client, one month, one PDF, read-only, human-reviewed. It builds on nothing in the library: Dossier serves founders mid-raise assembling diligence answers from their own files; Ledgerline serves agency principals assembling a defensible chronology of client-facing work from correspondence, a different buyer, a different artifact and a different trigger (an invoice dispute, not a data-room request). I held the score at 7.0 and the verdict at watch rather than dig_deeper because the two things I could not verify are the two that matter most: whether firms will hand over client mailboxes, and whether they will pay rather than write off disputed hours. I deliberately steered the venture away from the crowded AI-dev-tool bookmarks (Cursor Agent SDK, supermemory, multi-agent attribution) toward an operations buyer, as required — the sriramk 'who did what' bookmark informed the provenance idea but the agent-attribution product itself was dropped: Google is shipping per-agent identities in Workspace and Gmail/Calendar APIs do not expose which OAuth client created a record, so the technical foundation for a third-party version is missing.

Flatpack wins the build track on a different problem, for a different audience, from different bookmarks (the IKEA-instructions post and the /teardown skill, not the agent-infrastructure posts). It is the taste-file pattern: one input, a striking result in seconds, free, open source, screenshot-able. Its honest weakness is usefulness — you assemble furniture rarely — and its pain is latent: nobody says 'I need a manual parser', they just suffer silently on the floor, so the launch has to show the before/after rather than describe the problem. What would make people notice the pain is the side-by-side: the silent diagram next to the plain-English step with the screw count. I kept it clearly distinct from Partsy in the library (photo → one exploded diagram) by making the input a multi-page document and the output an ordered, tickable procedure with a hardware tally.

Neither idea reaches 7.5, so both are 'watch' — real but unproven. Both are filed since both clear 6.
candidates_considered:
VENTURE
1. Ledgerline — billable-work evidence trail for small agencies and consultancies. KEPT and selected: confirmed gap between quote-only enterprise passive timekeepers (Laurel, Smokeball AutoTime) and $10-25/seat agency PSA tools that only work if you logged it at the time; buyer owns the invoice.
2. Agent attribution layer for shared email/calendar ("who did what" across personal agents, from @sriramk). DROPPED: Google is shipping per-agent identities with their own Workspace accounts and audit trails, Gmail/Calendar APIs expose no creating-OAuth-client field, and the whole category is being absorbed by Workspace/Entra plus shadow-AI governance vendors (Push, Obsidian, Token Security). Also too close to the library's Driftwatch and Holdroom in buyer and theme.
3. Consent evidence vault for Messenger/SMS brand campaigns (from the Blueberry Broadcasts post + one-to-one consent rules). DROPPED as a lead: ActiveProspect TrustedForm already sells exactly this artifact at $0.15/certificate with a $10/mo self-serve minimum, and the platforms (Shopify Messaging, Attentive) do the pre-send screening — a well-funded player serving the same buyer with the same workflow at a fair price. Its evidence-artifact business model was carried over as the analogue for Ledgerline.
4. Agent-action reconciliation for clinic/home-services PMS and CRM records. DROPPED: real pain found (no vendor clearly demonstrates conflict detection or rollback for competing agent/staff edits), but it requires deep per-PMS integrations with Eaglesoft, eClinicalWorks and ServiceTitan — far past a solo builder's narrow first version, and the wedge would take months before one buyer could try it.

BUILD
1. Flatpack — manual PDF → tickable step deck with per-step hardware. KEPT and selected: dependencies all check out (PDF.js free, panels cropped from the user's own file, Gemini 3 Pro Image at $0.134/image, IKEA-Manual and IKEA-Bench datasets exist for validation); closest prior art is an unmaintained hackathon demo (ScrewYouIKEA) and chat-with-PDF tools that never produce a structured procedure.
2. Agent-config X-ray — paste an instructions.md / AGENTS.md / Cursor Agent SDK project and see the tool graph and capability surface. DROPPED as a repeat-adjacent: same audience and same core workflow as the library's Skillscope (paste an agent config, get a one-screen read on what it can do), just a different filename.
3. Thread → decision log: paste an email thread, get a dated record of what was agreed and by whom. DROPPED: good free versions already exist and are easy to find (ThreadSummary's 5 free summaries/month, Sotto's free notes generator, AI Emaily), and it shares its theme and audience with the Ledgerline venture, which the two-different-problems rule forbids.
4. Public dataset as a browsable shelf (taste-file pattern). DROPPED: I could not verify a specific fresh dataset that would make it newly possible this week, so freshness would score low and it would be a pretty page with no 'why now'.
research_notes:
22-call budget, 20 used. Reading pot (3/3): summarised supermemory's learner-1 (a cross-model memory layer, not weight-level continual learning — which killed my first read of that bookmark), the Cursor Agent SDK launch (markdown instructions + TypeScript tools + built-in evals + GitHub/Slack event triggers), and Blueberry Social Broadcasts (the 'upload your email list, find their Messenger profiles' claim is not confirmed on the vendor's own site, and Meta requires opt-in for marketing messages — so I treated the post as a prompt about consent evidence rather than a model to copy). I cannot see images; all three of those posts were video-only, so the summaries did the work.

Venture pot (11/12): searched agent identity/audit for email and calendar, which showed Google shipping per-agent Workspace identities (Oct 2026) and confirmed via the Calendar/Gmail API docs that no field exposes the creating OAuth client — this killed candidate 2 outright. Searched shadow-AI governance (Push, Obsidian, Token Security, Guardz) and found the enterprise end well covered. Researched TCPA one-to-one consent and found ActiveProspect TrustedForm's published pricing ($0.15/certificate, $10/mo minimum), which closed candidate 3 but gave me the evidence-artifact analogue I used in Ledgerline's comparables. Probed multi-agent ops pain in claims/billing/logistics (stale reads, conflicting writes, hard attribution) and clinic/home-services PMS write-backs (Yourcall, Echo Booking, Flexbone, Atty — none demonstrably reconcile conflicting edits), which was real but too integration-heavy. The decisive calls were the last three: automatic time capture (Laurel quote-only and enterprise-paced; Smokeball AutoTime Windows-only with no Google Workspace support; Clio Duo at $89-149/user/mo and legal-only) and agency PSA pricing (Teamwork $9.99/$24.99, Productive ~$9-10 with a 10-seat minimum, Scoro ~$17-19.90, Accelo quote-only). Those two calls reshaped the candidate from a vague 'agent audit trail' into the specific invoice-defence wedge and set the realistic price point.

Build pot (6/7): checked IKEA/manual prior art twice — found ScrewYouIKEA (unmaintained hackathon project), TalkingPDF and ManualScout (chat interfaces, iPhone-only in one case), and confirmed no free web tool produces a structured checklist with per-step parts and tools; also confirmed IKEA publishes assembly PDFs per product page but offers no API or archive, so v1 must be upload-only. Verified model economics twice: Gemini 3 Pro Image at $0.134 per 1K/2K image ($0.067 batched), no free API tier, and Google's own warning that generated labels can be wrong — which is exactly why the build plan crops real panels from the user's PDF instead of generating diagrams. Checked exploded-view/technical-illustration prior art and found only CLI skills and CAD tools, nothing consumer. Searched agent-config visualisers and thread-to-decision-log tools, both of which turned up enough free prior art (and overlap with the library or the venture) to drop them. Net effect of the research: the venture was reshaped from agent-attribution to agency invoice evidence, and the build was reshaped from 'generate a diagram' to 'crop the real diagram and generate only the words'.
prototype_summary: A clickable Ledgerline prototype that turns a messy month of Vantage Health client email into a dated, cited, scope-tagged evidence pack with exportable PDF chronology and invoice narrative.
